definition.text: A branch of statistics that deals with spatial or spatio-temporal data sets.

facts.text: It was first developed to predict the distribution of ore grades in mines and is now applied in soil science and in agriculture, especially precision farming.
Simpler interpolators such as inverse distance weighting came first; geostatistics goes further by treating values at unsampled places as correlated random variables.
A model of spatial continuity, often a parametric variogram, describes how strongly nearby values constrain the value at an unsampled point.
Using one spatial model across a whole area assumes stationarity, the same statistical properties everywhere; several methods relax that assumption.
It serves two goals: estimating the most likely value at each place, or simulating many alternative maps, called realizations, that together give probabilistic forecasts.
Bayesian inference plays a growing part, implementing kriging through a Gaussian process that is updated with Bayes' theorem.

definition.text: A graph or function describing how much pairs of observations differ according to the distance separating them, the key tool of geostatistics.

facts.text: Matheron defined the semivariogram in 1963 as half the average squared difference between values a distance h apart, the value being, for example, the iron content of soil.
Samples taken far apart vary more than samples taken close together.
Since nobody can sample everywhere, an empirical variogram is built from the squared differences between every pair of sample points, such as soil samples.
It is summarized by the nugget, a jump at the origin; the sill, its limit at large distances; and the range, where it nears the sill, often taken as 95% of it.
An empirical variogram is not guaranteed to be valid, so a model is fitted to it, most often linear, spherical, Gaussian or exponential.
The fitted variogram model sets the weights used in kriging.
Usage is muddled: some authors call the semivariogram a variogram, and the word semivariance can mislead.

definition.text: A geostatistical interpolation method that predicts a value at an unsampled point as a weighted average of nearby known values, based on a model of their covariance.

facts.text: Georges Matheron set out its theory in 1960, building on Danie Krige's thesis estimating gold grades from a few boreholes in South Africa's Witwatersrand.
Under suitable assumptions it gives the best linear unbiased prediction (BLUP) at unsampled locations.
Ordinary kriging chooses weights that minimize the mean squared error, with the weights summing to 1 so the estimate is unbiased.
Its estimation variance grows as samples lie farther from the target point and depends on the sampling layout, not on the sample values.
Only one realization of the random function is ever observed, so kriging must assume some degree of stationarity to infer its statistics.
Variants include simple kriging with a known mean, ordinary kriging with an unknown local mean, universal kriging with a trend, indicator kriging and co-kriging of related variables.
Its basic form is computationally heavy, but approximations scale it to larger problems.

definition.text: A spatial prediction technique that regresses the target variable on auxiliary variables, such as terrain and remote-sensing layers, and then kriges the regression residuals.

facts.text: It is mathematically equivalent to universal kriging and kriging with external drift.
It implements Matheron's 1969 universal model of spatial variation, in which deterministic and stochastic parts of variation are modelled separately.
The trend is fitted by ordinary or generalized least squares, then the residuals are interpolated by kriging and added back.
Pure regression and pure kriging are special cases: with no spatial autocorrelation it reduces to multiple regression, and with no useful covariates to ordinary kriging.
It is used to map the spatial distribution of soil properties, provided covariate layers exist that correlate significantly with the property.
Covariates keep multiplying: near-global topography at about 90 m from the 2000 Shuttle Radar Topography Mission, and MODIS images at 250 m.
Odeh and colleagues named it regression-kriging in 1995; Minasny and McBratney call it the empirical BLUP.
Minasny and McBratney found that more, better data matter more than more sophisticated statistics.

definition.text: The way a quantity measured at different places takes different values from place to place.

facts.text: It can be described with spatial descriptive statistics such as the range.
Variability is not uncertainty: a perfectly known field still varies, and uncertainty depends on sampling as well as on the amount of variability.
Geostatistics has been used to study how pesticide sorption and degradation vary across a field.
Geostatistical descriptions carry their own uncertainty, since variograms can be uncertain and interpolation methods differ.
Precision agriculture studies variability within fields, such as how terrain and soil properties affect crop growth and water distribution.
Urban landscapes and golf courses show high spatial variability in soil composition, unlike uniform farm fields.

definition.text: Estimating the values of a quantity at arbitrary places from values known at a set of points, when the variables are spatial coordinates.

facts.text: Geostatistics uses it to build digital elevation models from spot heights or survey depths.
Methods for scattered points include nearest-neighbour and natural-neighbour schemes, inverse distance weighting, kriging variants and thin-plate or other splines.
Gridding converts irregularly spaced data into a regular grid.
GIS software produces interpolated surfaces with methods such as inverse distance weighting, kriging, splines and trend surfaces.

definition.text: A deterministic interpolation method that estimates unknown values as a weighted average of known points, each weighted by the inverse of its distance.

facts.text: Donald Shepard, a Harvard freshman, published the method in 1968 while overhauling the interpolation in the SYMAP mapping program.
Shepard tested exponents of distance and settled near -2, close to the gravity model.
It was among the simpler interpolators known before geostatistics.
In Slovenia's Idrija area, it was used in GIS to turn soil samples into a raster map of mercury concentration.

definition.text: The science of measuring the shape of the land surface and the effects of that shape on human and natural processes.

facts.text: It extracts surface parameters and objects such as watersheds, stream networks and landforms from digital elevation models.
These parameters improve the mapping and modelling of soils, and serve precision agriculture and soil-landscape modelling.
Thanks largely to the Shuttle Radar Topography Mission and lidar, elevation models now cover almost all of Earth at 100 m resolution or better.
Slope, how steep the surface is, and aspect, the direction the slope faces, are its most basic derivatives.
Slope is computed from a raster model by discrete derivatives; the Horn method uses a cell and its eight neighbours.
Because water flows downhill, surface derivatives can predict surface stream flow.
Its ideas go back to Brisson (1808) and Gauss (1827), but it grew mainly with GIS and elevation data sets from the 1970s.

definition.text: A steady-state wetness index, computed from slope and upslope contributing area, that quantifies topographic control on hydrological processes.

facts.text: It combines the upslope area draining through a point per unit contour length with the local slope in radians.
Beven and Kirkby developed it within the TOPMODEL runoff model; it was designed for hillslope catenas and is not meaningful on flat ground.
It correlates highly with soil attributes such as horizon depth, silt percentage, organic matter content and phosphorus.
Areas with similar values become saturated under similar moisture conditions.

definition.text: A widely used remote-sensing measure of the health and density of vegetation, calculated from the red and near-infrared bands.

facts.text: Values run from -1 to 1: near zero means little or no vegetation, negative values mean water or non-land, and high values mean dense healthy vegetation.
Chlorophyll strongly absorbs visible light from 400 to 700 nm, while leaf cell structure strongly reflects near-infrared from 700 to 1100 nm.
Bare soils give small positive values of about 0.1 to 0.2, and because wet soil darkens, soil moisture changes can shift the index without any change in vegetation.
Alternatives such as the soil-adjusted vegetation index and the enhanced vegetation index correct for soil background effects.

definition.text: Imaging that captures data in a small number of separate wavelength bands, typically 3 to 15, including bands beyond visible light.

facts.text: Hyperspectral imaging differs by using often hundreds of contiguous bands.
A single multispectral image can show water depth, vegetation cover and soil moisture content.
Mid-infrared bands at 1550–1750 nm image vegetation and soil moisture, and far-infrared bands at 2080–2350 nm image soil, silicates and clays.
Surface and subsurface soil differ spectrally; disturbed soil emits more at 8.5 to 9.5 micrometres, which helps detect buried land mines.

definition.text: Imaging that records a full, finely resolved spectrum across many continuous bands for each pixel, to identify materials or detect processes.

facts.text: Materials leave characteristic spectral signatures that allow them to be identified.
Sensors on aircraft, satellites or drones are used to investigate plants and soils remotely, assessing ground cover and soil chemistry.
In farming it is being used to detect the nutrient and water status of wheat and heavy-metal stress in plants.
Although often treated as a surface technique, it can probe beneath the surface, to a depth set by the spectral range and the sample.

definition.text: A spectroscopic method using the near-infrared part of the spectrum, from 780 nm to 2500 nm.

facts.text: It rests on weak overtone and combination vibrations, so light penetrates deep into a sample and bulk material can be probed with little preparation.
Its broad, overlapping bands require multivariate calibration, such as principal components or partial least squares, built on carefully chosen calibration samples.
Karl Norris at the USDA pioneered it for agricultural products in the 1980s; it is valued as accurate, rapid, non-destructive and inexpensive.
Soil-testing laboratories may use near-infrared scanning.

definition.text: A geophysical method that images the subsurface with radar pulses, recording reflections from buried boundaries.

facts.text: It uses radio waves usually between 10 MHz and 2.6 GHz, reflected where materials of different permittivity meet.
It can reach up to 15 m in dry sandy soils but only a few centimetres in moist or clay-rich soils; higher frequencies trade penetration for resolution.
Clay soils and salt-contaminated soils limit it most, and rocky soils scatter the signal.
It is used to study soils and bedrock, and cross-borehole radar assesses the presence and amount of soil water.

definition.text: A geophysical technique that images subsurface structure from electrical resistivity measured with electrodes at the surface or in boreholes.

facts.text: Current is passed between two outer electrodes in a line of four, voltage is read between the inner two, and a geometric factor converts the result to apparent resistivity.
Wetter soil is less resistive, dry and saturated soil can differ by orders of magnitude, and clays conduct through charged particle surfaces as well as pore water.
Electrode spacings of 0.75 to 12.0 m serve shallow surveys under 10 m, and depth is usually less than the widest spacing.
It maps soil moisture for precision agriculture, images root zones and tracks contaminants in soil and groundwater.

definition.text: The use of orbiting gamma-ray spectrometers to map the elements of planetary surfaces, especially the Moon and Mars.

facts.text: Cosmic rays strike nuclei in the soil, releasing neutrons and exciting nuclei that then emit gamma rays of characteristic energy.
The energy of each emission line identifies an element and its intensity gives the concentration; about 20 elements can be measured.
Neutron detectors sense hydrogen in the upper metre of the surface, revealing water ice; Mars Odyssey carried one with two neutron detectors.
Mapping from orbit fails for bodies with thick atmospheres such as Earth and Venus.

title: SoilGrids

definition.text: A system for automated global soil mapping based on models fitted to soil profiles and environmental covariate data.

facts.text: ISRIC produces its world maps of soil properties at 250 m cells, with quantified uncertainty, by machine learning on the WoSIS profile database and over 400 global covariates.
It and the WoSIS database are ISRIC's flagship soil information products.

related: International Soil Reference and Information Centre

definition.text: Chemometrics is the science of extracting information from chemical systems by data-driven means.

facts.text: It draws on multivariate statistics, applied mathematics and computer science to solve problems in chemistry, biology, medicine and engineering.
Svante Wold coined the term in a 1971 grant application, and the field emerged in the 1970s as computers came into scientific use.
Infrared and UV/visible spectra contain thousands of measurements per sample, but strong low-rank structure lets principal components analysis and partial least squares model them compactly.
Chemometric models are usually judged by root mean squared error of prediction, and model selection relies on resampling such as bootstrap, permutation and cross-validation.

definition.text: Multivariate calibration builds models that predict a property of interest from measured responses such as spectra.

facts.text: A training set pairs reference values (for example analyte concentration) with the measured spectra; partial least squares or principal component regression then relates response to property.
Methods are classed as classical, which optimally describe the measured responses, or inverse, which need less physical knowledge and usually predict better in mean-squared-error terms.
It lets fast, cheap, non-destructive measurements estimate properties that would otherwise need slow or costly analysis, even under heavy interference from other analytes.
Broad, non-selective near-infrared spectra can still predict properties when paired with carefully developed calibration, because selectivity comes partly from the mathematics.

definition.text: Compositional data are quantitative descriptions of the parts of some whole, conveying relative information.

facts.text: They are represented as points on a simplex; proportions, percentages and ppm all count as compositional data.
Closure divides each part by the total, so only the ratios between components carry information and scaling by any positive constant changes nothing.
John Aitchison defined compositional data as proportions of some whole in 1982.
Three-part compositions are plotted on a ternary (barycentric) triangle showing the ratios of the three variables as a position.
Examples include molar concentrations in chemistry and mineral fractions of a rock in geology.

title: Log-ratio transformation

definition.text: Log-ratio transformations map compositions from the simplex into real space so ordinary statistics can be applied.

facts.text: The additive log ratio (alr) takes logs of ratios to one arbitrarily chosen component; it is common in chemistry (pH) and multinomial logistic regression but is not an isometry.
The centred log ratio (clr) is an isomorphism and isometry, but it forces a linear dependency so the covariance matrix is singular.
The isometric log ratio (ilr) gives orthonormal coordinates in D-1 dimensions, built by Gram-Schmidt, singular-value decomposition or a bifurcating tree.
The article argues that noise distorts compositions asymmetrically, so ilr can create artifacts in real data.

notes: Wikipedia page contains a contested argument against ILR; sentences 8fec84c5bfed onward are one author's position.

title: Electromagnetic induction

definition.text: Electromagnetic induction is the production of an electromotive force across a conductor in a changing magnetic field.

facts.text: Faraday published its discovery in 1831 and Joseph Henry found it independently in 1832; Maxwell later described it mathematically.
Faraday's law says the induced emf in a closed circuit equals the rate of change of enclosed magnetic flux, and Lenz's law says the induced current opposes the change that produced it.
A changing current in one wire induces an emf in a second wire within reach of its magnetic field, which is the principle of the transformer.
Conductors in changing magnetic fields develop circular eddy currents in planes perpendicular to the field.

notes: Physics background for electromagnetic-induction soil sensors; the sentences here do not mention soil.

definition.text: Fuzzy clustering, also called soft clustering, is a form of clustering in which each data point can belong to more than one cluster.

facts.text: In hard clustering each point belongs to exactly one cluster, while fuzzy clustering gives each point a membership grade for every cluster; points at a cluster's edge have lower grades.
Fuzzy c-means, developed by Dunn in 1973 and improved by Bezdek in 1981, alternates computing membership-weighted centroids with updating each point's coefficients until they converge.
A parameter m controls fuzziness: larger m gives fuzzier clusters, m near 1 reduces to k-means, and m is commonly set to 2 without other knowledge.
Like k-means, it finds only a local minimum that depends on the initial weights.

definition.text: The Landsat program is the longest-running enterprise that has acquired satellite imagery of Earth.

facts.text: The first satellite launched on 23 July 1972 as the Earth Resources Technology Satellite and was renamed Landsat 1 in 1975; Landsat 9 launched on 27 September 2021.
Landsat 7 data has eight spectral bands with spatial resolutions from 15 to 60 m and a temporal resolution of 16 days; a scene is about 185 km by 185 km.

Instruments progressed from the Multispectral Scanner (Landsat 1-5) to the Thematic Mapper, the Enhanced Thematic Mapper Plus (Landsat 7) and, on Landsat 8, the Operational Land Imager plus a Thermal Infrared Sensor.
Landsat gives one of the longest uninterrupted remote-sensing time series, from 1972 to the present, and is widely used for land-cover determination.

definition.text: Latin hypercube sampling (LHS) is a statistical method for generating a near-random sample of parameter values from a multidimensional distribution.

facts.text: The range of each variable is split into M equally probable intervals and M points are placed so each interval of every variable holds exactly one point, like non-attacking rooks on a chess board.
It needs no more samples for more variables, and samples can be taken in sequence while remembering which cells were already used.
Unlike plain random sampling, the number of points must be chosen beforehand, but every subspace is then sampled with equal density.

definition.text: The modifiable areal unit problem (MAUP) is a source of statistical bias that arises when point-based measures are aggregated into areal units.

facts.text: Summary values depend on both the shape and the scale of the aggregation unit, so results differ between, say, state and county boundaries.
The scale effect changes results between aggregation levels (correlation generally rises as unit size rises); the zoning effect changes them when data are regrouped at the same scale.
Gehlke and Biehl first recognised it in 1934 and Openshaw described it in detail in 1984; it is closely related to ecological fallacy.
Aggregation can hide a strong correlation or create a spurious one, so sensitivity analysis with several areal units is recommended to estimate the uncertainty of coefficients.

definition.text: Partial least squares (PLS) regression is a reduced-rank method that projects both predictors and responses into new spaces to find the relation between them.

facts.text: It looks for the direction in predictor space that explains maximum variance in response space, modelling the covariance structure of two matrices with latent variables.
It suits data with more variables than observations or with multicollinearity among predictors, where standard regression fails unless regularised.
Herman Wold introduced it, with his son Svante Wold, first in the social sciences; it is now most widely used in chemometrics.
Components are extracted iteratively by finding directions of maximal covariance and regressing on the scores; PLS1 handles a single response vector and PLS-DA a categorical one.

definition.text: Random forest is an ensemble learning method for classification and regression that builds many decision trees during training.

facts.text: Classification returns the class chosen by most trees; regression returns the average of the trees' predictions, which corrects decision trees' habit of overfitting.

Each tree is trained on a bootstrap sample drawn with replacement (bagging), and each split considers only a random subset of features, which decorrelates trees when a few features are very strong predictors.
Tin Kam Ho created the first algorithm in 1995; Breiman and Cutler extended it.
Variable importance can be ranked by permutation: permute a feature in the out-of-bag samples and see how much the error rises, or by mean decrease in impurity.
The cost of higher accuracy than a single tree is lost interpretability.

title: Sampling design

definition.text: A sampling design specifies for every possible sample its probability of being drawn.

facts.text: It is written as a function P(S) giving the probability of drawing sample S; Bernoulli sampling is one example.
Designing a sample means defining the population, sampling frame and sampling unit, the margin of error to achieve, and how to balance sampling and non-sampling error.

notes: thin: no soil-specific design (grid, stratified, conditioned Latin hypercube) in these sentences.

definition.text: Spatial analysis is any of the formal techniques that study entities using their topological, geometric or geographic properties.

facts.text: It spans many methods, especially spatial statistics, and covers spatial interpolation, spatial regression and spatial autocorrelation statistics such as Moran's I and Geary's C.
Geographic information systems capture, store, manipulate and analyse spatial data, with map overlay a basic vector operation.
Common errors include the ecological fallacy (drawing conclusions about individuals from aggregate data) and the locational fallacy (a poor spatial characterisation of the elements).
Spatial sampling picks limited locations to measure phenomena that show dependency and heterogeneity; basic schemes are random, clustered and systematic.

title: Spatial autocorrelation
article: Spatial analysis#Fundamental issues > Spatial dependence > Spatial auto-correlation

definition.text: Spatial dependency is the co-variation of properties across geographic space, so characteristics at nearby locations appear correlated, positively or negatively.

facts.text: It produces the spatial autocorrelation problem, which violates standard statistical techniques that assume independent observations.

Dependence means one location can predict another, so observations are not needed at both; heterogeneity means the relation changes across space, so an observed dependence cannot be trusted beyond a possibly small region.
Classic statistics include Moran's I, Geary's C and Getis's G.

definition.text: Spatial scale describes or categorises the size of a space, or the extent at which a phenomenon or process occurs.

facts.text: A common geography and meteorology scheme runs from micro (1 m to 1 km, local) through meso (1 to 100 km, regional) and macro (100 to 10,000 km, continental) to mega (global) and giga (superglobal).
These divisions are somewhat arbitrary and shift by context, so meso and macro must be adjusted accordingly.

definition.text: Stratified sampling samples a population that can be partitioned into subpopulations by sampling each stratum independently.

facts.text: Strata must be collectively exhaustive and mutually exclusive, so every element falls in exactly one; sampling inside each, for example by simple random sampling, improves precision by reducing sampling error.
Proportionate allocation samples each stratum in proportion to its size; optimum allocation takes larger samples where variability is greatest, and Neyman allocation is one such strategy.
It gives a smaller estimation error when within-strata standard deviation is lower than the overall one, and it ensures enough samples from strata of interest.
Combining sub-strata to reach adequate numbers can cause Simpson's paradox, in which trends disappear or reverse.

title: Uncertainty quantification

definition.text: Uncertainty quantification is the science of quantitatively characterising and estimating uncertainties in computational and real-world applications.

facts.text: It tries to determine how likely outcomes are when some aspects of a system are not exactly known.

Forward propagation pushes input uncertainty through a model to get the output's mean and variance, reliability or full distribution; inverse quantification estimates the discrepancy between model and experiment and unknown parameters.
Forward methods include Monte Carlo simulation, surrogate models, local and functional expansions and first/second-order reliability methods.
Inverse problems are harder and face dimensionality and identifiability issues, since different parameter and discrepancy combinations can give the same prediction.

notes: General (non-soil) treatment; soil-mapping uncertainty (prediction intervals) not covered by these sentences.

definition.text: The scorpan model, proposed by McBratney and colleagues in 2003, extends Jenny's clorpt model so that soil-environment relationships can be applied digitally.

facts.text: It keeps climate, organisms, relief, parent material and age, and adds s (intrinsic soil properties captured by remote and proximal sensors) and n (spatial coordinates or position relative to a geographic phenomenon).
A quantitative function f links individual scorpan factors, or a combination, to the soil property or class being predicted.
Its strength is flexibility: it combines existing soil surveys with remote sensing, elevation, climate, land use and geology data, all as raster layers re-projected to one projection and resolution.

Relief (usually from a digital elevation model) is the most used factor in digital soil mapping, soil is second, and climate one of the least used, partly because topography proxies for local climate.
Age is rarely used because soil age is hard to put into a GIS-friendly form; the position factor can use sample coordinates or distance to a feature.
Pedometrics applies mathematical and statistical methods to the distribution and genesis of soils; DSM techniques date from the 1970s, and technology made them practical products since the 2000s.
A map needs three ingredients: environmental layers representing scorpan factors, geo-referenced soil data, and a model relating soil to environment to predict at unsampled locations.
It is usually supervised learning: sample locations are intersected with the environmental layers to build a training set, a fitted classification or regression function is then applied to all cells.

definition.text: Conventional soil mapping is the surveyor-led production of soil maps from field inspections, building on Jenny's soil-forming factors and national taxonomic systems.

facts.text: The steps are objectives, background compilation and initial legend, then soil inspections, field mapping and correlation, and finally map production and a report.
Soils are represented as a profile, a 1-3 m wide pedon, a polypedon of connected similar pedons, or a map unit, the polygon mapped by surveyors.
Choropleth maps assume each map unit is homogeneous, yet units contain inclusions of minor soils too small to map, and real soil change is often a fuzzy gradation rather than a sharp boundary.
Raising map-unit purity raises cost exponentially, and maps made for different objectives leave mismatched boundaries and inconsistent series names across counties and provinces.
Legacy maps still hold decades of surveyor knowledge and serve as training data for digital soil maps.

title: Soil survey intensity levels
article: doc>geo.libretexts.org/Bookshelves/Soil_Science/Digging_into_Canadian_Soils%3A_An_Introduction_to_Soil_Science/03%3A_Digging_Deeper/3.04%3A_Digital_Soil_Mapping#CONVENTIONAL SOIL MAPPING > Table 17.1. Soil survey intensity level guidelines adapted from Mapping Systems Working Group (1981)

definition.text: Survey intensity levels grade how densely a conventional soil survey is checked in the field.

facts.text: Level 1, very detailed, needs one inspection per polygon with foot traverses under 0.5 km apart, published at 1:5,000 at series level.
Level 2, detailed, inspects over 90% of polygons with traverses 2 km apart at 1:20,000; level 3, reconnaissance, inspects 60-80% with traverses 4 km apart at 1:50,000.

notes: thin: only levels 1-3 of the table seen in the dossier.

title: Soil sampling design for digital soil mapping

definition.text: Sampling design for digital soil mapping selects sites representative of the geographic area and of the soil-forming factors (covariates) being modelled.

facts.text: Geometric designs include grid, simple random, stratified random, transect, cluster and nested sampling; grid sampling places points at the centre of evenly spaced cells, and stratified random applies random sampling within strata.
Cluster sampling groups sites closely to cope with rough terrain, and nested sampling quantifies variability at different distances.

Feature-space designs use covariate values: fuzzy k-means sampling minimises distance in covariate space, and conditioned Latin hypercube sampling (Minasny and McBratney, 2006) samples all covariates with one sample per stratum.
An optimal design covers both geographic and feature space.

definition.text: Accuracy assessment measures how far a digital soil map's predicted values differ from observed ones, using an independent validation dataset.

facts.text: Categorical predictions use overall accuracy (share correctly predicted) and Cohen's kappa, which corrects for chance agreement; both range from 0 to 1.
Continuous predictions use mean square error, root mean square error (in the soil variable's units), R2 and Lin's concordance correlation coefficient; lower MSE or RMSE means a more accurate model.
R2 is not accuracy because it ignores bias from systematic over- or underprediction; the concordance coefficient, which measures fit to the 45-degree line, is more appropriate.

definition.text: Digital soil map uncertainty is the error that accumulates in a predicted soil map, which should be estimated as carefully as it is validated.

facts.text: It comes from three sources: the measured soil property, the environmental predictors, and the predictive model.
Property errors arise from laboratory methods, pedotransfer functions and GPS location accuracy; predictor errors from DEM vertical error, sensor error and polygon boundaries and scale.
Model structure matters because linear, non-linear and hybrid models (such as model trees) capture different soil-environment relationships.
International standards such as GlobalSoilMap require a 90% prediction interval map with 5% and 95% limits; a wider interval means higher uncertainty, and this applies only to continuous variables.
